messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  (none)

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  (none)

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Milan had been working as a salesperson in a busy retail corridor when the shelling began in his city, first as a distant, almost unplaceable thud and then as a violent series of blasts that sent people running into doorways and stairwells. He had been on his phone with his girlfriend, telling her he was heading home, when the windows in the storefront across from him shattered and the street filled with dust, screaming, and the sharp smell of smoke. For a few seconds he stood frozen, then crouched behind a display table with two coworkers while the building shook again. What stayed with him was not only the noise but the feeling that the ordinary world had turned against him without warning, that the next explosion could land anywhere, and that he had no way to protect himself or the people he cared about. Afterward, when he finally got back to the apartment he shared with his girlfriend, he could not stop replaying the scene in his mind, sure that he should have moved faster, chosen a different route, done something more useful. The horror of that afternoon left him with a deep, nauseating fear and a sense of guilt that he had survived by chance rather than by any strength of his own.

In the weeks that followed, Milan began to live as if danger were only a thin wall away. Even after he was able to return to work, he found that the brightness and chatter of the sales floor did not settle him; instead, his attention kept snapping away from customers and toward every sudden sound from the street. He had trouble concentrating on simple tasks like remembering prices, answering questions, or finishing a stock count, because part of him was always scanning for the next impact. He became especially uneasy at night, when the city was quieter and the darkness made every distant bang feel closer and more ominous. He would lie awake listening for sirens or the rumble of vehicles, and if he did fall asleep, he woke easily at the smallest noise. His girlfriend noticed that he often asked her to check the locks twice and that he sat with his back to the wall in restaurants, but he did not say that what frightened him most was the feeling that safety had become temporary and unreliable.

Over time, Milan’s fear and shame narrowed his life. He began avoiding the busiest streets on his commute and leaving work early when the light faded, telling himself he was being practical, though he knew he was really trying to keep the day from turning into another version of that afternoon. At the shop, he pushed through customer interactions with a strained politeness, but his mind wandered so often that he missed details and had to ask people to repeat themselves, which made him feel embarrassed and more on edge. At home, the evenings became a struggle: he kept the television low, scanned the windows before drawing the curtains, and sat awake beside his girlfriend long after she had gone to bed. The night vigilance fed his exhaustion, and the exhaustion made it even harder for him to focus at work, which in turn left him feeling that he was failing at the one role he had been trying hardest to preserve. He hated how often fear, anger, and guilt surged together—fear at the possibility of another strike, anger at the war and at the helplessness it had forced on him, guilt that he still had a life to complain about when others had lost theirs. Even small reminders, like a sudden slam from the back room or a passing siren outside the store, could wash over him with the same old horror, and he would feel his body tighten before he could think. By the time he sought help, his PCL-5 score reflected how consuming it had become. He came in because his girlfriend told him she could see how little rest he was getting and how far away he seemed, and because he was afraid that if he kept living this way he would lose his job, lose his ability to concentrate, and lose the sense that night could ever be safe again.
